The lyric uses the word 'suicide' to describe the political act of sending young people to die in a war that is no longer being defended on its original terms. The song's argument is that this kind of sustained policy choice is functionally suicidal at the level of a national body, even if no individual involved is suicidal.

The arrangement is one of the most direct three-minute rock songs on Pearl Jam. The verse is built on a tight, forward-driving riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. The song is structurally simple, deliberately so: Vedder has said in interviews that he wanted the song to feel like a leaflet rather than like a poem. McCready's solo at the song's center is a short, controlled scream rather than an extended melodic piece.

The song won the Grammy for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals at the 2007 ceremony, the only Grammy Pearl Jam has won. Vedder did not attend the ceremony to receive the award. The band's distance from the Grammy infrastructure has been a long-standing feature of their public posture, and the 'World Wide Suicide' Grammy was therefore received and then largely set aside by the band.

In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'World Wide Suicide' was played at Morumbi on November 3 (fifth in the running order) and at Curitiba on November 9 (seventeenth). The Bush administration had ended in January 2009 and the Iraq War had been officially declared over by the Obama administration in December 2011, just weeks after these shows. The song's placement in the 2011 setlists therefore carried a specific meaning: it was a retrospective rather than a current statement, an artifact of a political moment that the band was acknowledging had ended without quite ending. The Brazilian audience response to the song was the response of an audience whose own politics had been shaped by hostility to the Bush-era United States.
unthought known:
'Unthought Known' is the seventh track on Backspacer (2009), the album where Pearl Jam concluded its long retreat from mainstream visibility and made, for the first time since Yield, music that was not designed to repel a casual listener. The music is Vedder's (a rare solo music credit on a Pearl Jam album); the lyric is also Vedder's. The song is a meditation on intuition, on the kind of emotional knowledge that arrives without permission and that resists being articulated as thought.

The phrase 'unthought known' is borrowed from the work of the British psychoanalyst Christopher Bollas, whose 1987 book The Shadow of the Object: Psychoanalysis of the Unthought Known introduces the concept of psychic content that the subject knows without ever having thought it. Vedder has cited Bollas as the source of the phrase in a 2009 interview promoting Backspacer with Spin. The song therefore carries an unusual epistemological argument for a rock track: it claims that the most important things a person knows are the things they have never been able to put into words, and that the work of being alive is to honor that unspoken knowledge rather than to forcibly translate it.

The arrangement is one of the most patient on Backspacer. The verse is built on a slow piano figure (Vedder plays the piano on the recording; Stone Gossard adds guitar texture beneath) that resolves through the chorus into a wider sound. Matt Cameron's drumming holds the song's tempo steady throughout, refusing the kind of release that other Backspacer tracks deploy. McCready's solo at the climax is unusually melodic, closer to a Mike Campbell line than to a McCready signature.

Live, the song became one of the most consistent late-set placements on Pearl Jam tours from 2009 onward. The audience-led wordless vocal that the band invites during the chorus is one of the reliable communal moments in the post-Backspacer touring catalog. By 2011 the song had earned its place in setlists alongside the older anthems; audiences had learned the wordless chorus and could carry it without prompting.

In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Unthought Known' appeared three times. At Morumbi on November 3 it was placed eighth in the running order. At Apoteose on November 6 it opened the show, the first song of the Rio night. At Curitiba on November 9 it was placed twenty-first. The varying placements across the four shows is unusual; the band tends to find a position for a song on a tour and stay with it. The fact that 'Unthought Known' moved between opener, mid-set anchor, and late-set release across the four Brazilian dates suggests the band was using the song as a tonal flex point, deploying it wherever it was needed rather than where it had been preplanned. The Apoteose opener is the most interesting of the three placements: opening a show with a song this slow and this internal is one of the more confident sequencing decisions on the South American Tour 2011 bootleg recordings.
whipping:
'Whipping' is the sixth track on Vitalogy (1994). The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the angriest things on a Pearl Jam record that contains many angry things, and one of the few songs in the catalog where the political target is specifically reproductive rights and the women who put their bodies between the law and the choice. The song is a companion piece to 'Porch' on Ten, written three years later, after the political ground had shifted further.

Vitalogy was recorded between November 1993 and April 1994, in the period when the murders of abortion providers had begun in earnest in the United States. Dr. David Gunn was killed in Florida in March 1993; Dr. John Britton and James Barrett were killed in Florida in July 1994; Shannon Lowney and Lee Ann Nichols were killed in Massachusetts in December 1994. 'Whipping' was written during this rising violence, and the song's anger is the anger of someone watching a movement turn its rhetoric into murder. Vedder has discussed the song's context in a 1994 Spin interview that ran during the Vitalogy promotional cycle.

The lyric is more abstract than 'Porch' but more focused. Where 'Porch' addresses bodily autonomy as a question, 'Whipping' addresses the political reaction to that autonomy as a fact. The narrator is observing the violence from a critical distance and refusing to be neutral about it. The song does not name the providers or the victims, which is consistent with how Vedder writes about specific events: the lyric is a posture rather than a memorial.

The arrangement is one of the shortest songs on Vitalogy, less than two and a half minutes. The verse is a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus is a single-line declaration that the band repeats with rising volume. Matt Cameron had not yet joined the band at this point (Dave Abbruzzese was still the drummer for the Vitalogy sessions), and Abbruzzese's drumming on 'Whipping' is among the most punishing of his Pearl Jam tenure. The song was recorded quickly, in fewer than a dozen takes, and the recording's roughness is a feature.

Live, 'Whipping' has been a regular but not constant setlist presence. The song works best when the band wants to inject a high-velocity political moment into a show; it does not work as a closer or as a slow-build piece. In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Whipping' appeared at Morumbi on November 3, ninth in the running order, between 'Unthought Known' and 'Daughter.' The placement is one of the South American Tour 2011 sequencing fingerprints: the band was using Vitalogy political tracks in the second quarter of shows, where the audience had been warmed up enough by Ten and Vs. material to receive the heavier argument. The Morumbi audience response to 'Whipping' is brisker than the response to 'Unthought Known' that preceded it, which is consistent with how Brazilian audiences had received Vitalogy political material since the 1990s.
daughter:
'Daughter' is the third track on Vs. (1993). The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most direct pieces of writing in the early Pearl Jam catalog about the intersection of childhood, learning disability, and family violence. The narrator is observing a girl whose unspecified neurodivergence (the lyric implies dyslexia or another reading-related condition without naming it) is being met with shame and anger by her parents rather than with care. The song is the band's most explicit early statement that the home is, for some children, the most dangerous place in their lives.

Vedder has discussed the song's origin across multiple interviews from the Vs. promotional cycle. The most cited account is from a 1993 Rolling Stone conversation: Vedder had read about the way some learning-disabled children were treated in American school systems and households in the 1980s and early 1990s, and the song is his composite response. The narrator does not name the girl, does not name the disability, and does not editorialize. The song's argument is structural rather than rhetorical: the audience is asked to listen and to draw the obvious conclusion.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most economical pieces of writing. The verse is built on a single-string acoustic figure that resolves into a fuller arrangement in the chorus; the bridge introduces a harmonic shift that the song does not return from. Matt Cameron had not yet joined the band when Vs. was recorded; Dave Abbruzzese plays drums, and his work on 'Daughter' is some of the most restrained of his Pearl Jam tenure. The song's restraint is the source of its emotional weight.

Live, 'Daughter' has been one of Pearl Jam's primary tag songs since the mid-1990s. The closing minute of the live arrangement opens up into space where the band routinely insert fragments of other songs (the most famous is 'It's OK,' the Dead Moon song; 'Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2' has appeared frequently since the 2010s; W.M.A. has been used in some performances). The 'Daughter' tag is therefore one of the band's most flexible improvisational vehicles, and any given live recording of the song can be identified by which tag was attached.

In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Daughter' appeared at Morumbi on November 3 (tenth in the order, with W.M.A. as the tag), and at Apoteose on November 6 (ninth in the order). The W.M.A. tag at Morumbi is one of the more interesting tag choices on the South American Tour 2011 bootlegs, because it pairs the song's domestic-violence subject with the police-violence subject of W.M.A. directly. The two songs are stylistically and harmonically incompatible (W.M.A. is one of Vs.'s most aggressive moments, 'Daughter' one of its most restrained), and the band's decision to fuse them on this particular night is one of the show's signal moments.
elderly woman behind the counter in a sm:
Often abbreviated to 'Small Town' on bootleg lists and on the Pearl Jam audio recording channel, 'Elderly Woman Behind the Counter in a Small Town' is the seventh track on Vs. (1993). The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The full title is a deliberate satire of the brevity-obsessed title conventions of mainstream rock radio in 1993: the band gave the song the longest title that would fit on a CD case, knowing that this would force radio DJs and chart writers to either say the title in full or to abbreviate it in a way that would always be visibly partial. Both choices ridicule the medium that the song was being delivered through.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most patient pieces of writing. The narrator is the woman of the title, an elderly cashier in a small town who is reflecting on a life of having stayed where she was born while her former lover left and built a different life elsewhere. The song does not editorialize about either choice. It documents the woman's interior reasoning in the present moment and lets the listener observe both the ache and the integrity of the decision to stay. This is the kind of fully-imagined-other-person lyric that Vedder occasionally pulled off in the early 1990s and that the band would more rarely attempt later.

The arrangement is the most folk-inflected thing on Vs. The verse is built on an acoustic guitar figure that does not vary; the chorus opens into a harmony that Vedder doubles in his own voice. Stone Gossard has cited Neil Young as the model for this kind of writing, and the song's structural patience (it does not lift the way the album's harder rockers do) is a deliberate inheritance from Young. McCready's solo at the song's center is twelve bars and unusually melodic; on the studio recording it is closer in spirit to a country-rock turn than to a grunge solo.

Live, the song has been one of the band's most reliable singalongs for over thirty years. The chorus is invariably carried by the audience, with Vedder stepping back from the microphone for entire phrases. The song occupies a specific position in setlists: it is almost always placed in the first third of a show, where it functions as the first communal moment of the night, and where its slow tempo prepares the audience for whatever the band is about to escalate into. By the late 2000s the song had become so reliable in this role that audiences would begin singing the opening line before the first guitar chord arrived.

In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Elderly Woman' appeared in three of the four nights. At Morumbi on November 4 (the second SP show) it was placed sixth in the order. At Apoteose on November 6 it was placed fifteenth. At Curitiba on November 9 it was placed sixth. The placement at Curitiba is the most canonical (early-set communal moment); the placement at Apoteose is unusual and reflects the Rio show's tendency to delay singalongs until deeper into the set. The Brazilian audience response across the four shows is one of the most consistent on the bootleg recordings; the chorus singalong is fully carried by the audience in each case.
wishlist:
'Wishlist' is the eighth track on Yield (1998). The music is Vedder's (a solo music credit, unusual for a Pearl Jam song from this period); the lyric is also Vedder's. The song is structurally the simplest thing on Yield: a single verse pattern that repeats while Vedder lists the things the narrator wishes he could be. The list never resolves into a concluding statement, and the song ends with the narrator still wishing. The structure is the argument: wishing is not a precursor to action, it is its own state, and the song honors the state without trying to convert it into anything else.

The lyric was written quickly, by Vedder's own description in the 1998 Yield press cycle. He has framed the song in interviews from the period as a kind of automatic writing, a list of metaphorical positions he found himself wanting to occupy on a given afternoon. The song does not require interpretation in the traditional sense; the wishes are the meaning. This refusal to layer meaning on top of the literal text is unusual for Vedder and is part of why 'Wishlist' has been read by some critics as the most innocent thing he ever recorded.

The arrangement is one of the most pared-down on Yield. The verse is built on three chords played gently by Vedder on acoustic guitar; the band enters under the second verse and remains restrained throughout. Mike McCready's solo, when it arrives at the end of the song, is the only moment where the arrangement raises its volume above conversational. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is, by Cameron's own description in PJ20, the lightest he had ever played on a Pearl Jam track up to that point.

The song was the second single from Yield, released in May 1998, and reached the top thirty on the Billboard Modern Rock chart. Its commercial reception was warm but not enormous. The song's enduring presence in Pearl Jam shows is therefore not the residue of a hit; it is the residue of audience attachment to the song's tone. Audiences began singing along to the song's verse-by-verse structure during the Yield tour and have continued doing so consistently through every subsequent Pearl Jam tour cycle.

In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Wishlist' appeared at Morumbi on November 4 (the second SP show, ninth in the order). The placement is canonical: a slow song in the early-middle of a set, where the audience has been warmed up enough to settle into a communal singalong. The Brazilian audience response to the song on the Morumbi bootleg is one of the more emotional moments of the night, with audible weeping audible in the recording during the second verse. South American Tour 2011 setlists tended to use 'Wishlist' as a stillness marker; the song's appearances are predictable and consistent in their placement.
just breathe:
'Just Breathe' is the fifth track on Backspacer (2009) and the most commercially successful Pearl Jam song since 'Last Kiss.' Vedder wrote both the music and the lyric. The song was released as the second single from the album in October 2009 and reached the top forty on the Billboard Hot 100, the band's highest chart position for an original composition since 'Better Man' had charted on rock radio fifteen years earlier. The song is a love declaration written by a man who is more aware of how much he might lose than of how much he has.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most domestic pieces of writing. The narrator is reflecting on his relationship with a partner, on the fact of being lucky to have her, on the shadow of mortality that hovers over every couple's life together. The song was written during the Backspacer sessions in 2008 and 2009, in a period when Vedder had recently become a father (his daughter Olivia was born in 2004; his daughter Harper was born in 2008) and when he was openly framing his own writing as having shifted toward gratitude and away from rage. 'Just Breathe' is the most direct fingerprint of that shift in the catalog.

The melody and the chord progression are heavily indebted to Vedder's 2007 Into the Wild soundtrack, particularly to 'Tuolumne' and 'Society.' Vedder has discussed in interviews from the Backspacer period (a 2009 Rolling Stone conversation is the most cited) that he had been writing more on acoustic guitar since Into the Wild, and that 'Just Breathe' was one of the songs that survived the transition from solo material to band material. Glen Hansard, who collaborated with Vedder on Into the Wild, contributed background vocals to the studio recording.

The arrangement is one of the most pared-down on Backspacer. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure; the band enters under the second verse but stays restrained. Matt Cameron plays brushes rather than sticks for most of the song. Mike McCready does not play a solo. Stone Gossard's contribution is a single layer of pedal steel-style guitar that floats under the chorus. The arrangement honors the lyric's intimacy by refusing to scale up to a stadium-sized release.

Live, 'Just Breathe' has been a setlist regular since 2009. The song occupies a specific position: it is almost always placed in the latter half of a set, where it functions as the show's emotional pause before the closing surge. Vedder typically performs the song with reduced lighting and a stripped-down arrangement that mirrors the studio recording's restraint. In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Just Breathe' appeared at Morumbi on November 3 (nineteenth in the order, deep in the encore), at Morumbi on November 4 (nineteenth again), at Apoteose on November 6 (eighteenth), and at Curitiba on November 9 (twentieth). The consistent placement across all four nights signals the band had decided in advance that the song would mark the encore's intimate center on this tour. Brazilian audience responses across the four bootlegs are uniformly hushed during the song and explosive after.
got some:
'Got Some' is the second track on Backspacer (2009), the album's most aggressive immediate burst, and the song that most cleanly bridges Vedder's late-2000s political concerns and the band's instinct toward direct three-minute rock writing. The music is credited collectively to Pearl Jam; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was Backspacer's lead-off statement after the opener 'Gonna See My Friend' and is a sustained appeal for relief from the cumulative exhaustion of the post-9/11 American decade.

The lyric works as a list. The narrator is asking, in compressed punk-style address, for a specific kind of mercy: an honest answer, a relief from cynicism, a remedy for the cumulative spiritual erosion that the Bush years and the financial crisis of 2008 had imposed on the American public. The song was written during the Backspacer sessions in late 2008 and early 2009, in the immediate aftermath of the Obama election; the song's relief is the relief of someone who has not yet fully believed that the bad period is over and is asking for confirmation that it is.

Musically, 'Got Some' is one of the shortest songs on Backspacer (under three minutes) and one of the fastest. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging. McCready's solo is a controlled six-bar burst rather than an extended melodic statement. The song was produced by Brendan O'Brien, who has produced the majority of Pearl Jam's albums since Vs., and his preference for tight rhythm-section recording is audible across the track.

The song was released as a 7-inch vinyl single accompanying Target Stores copies of Backspacer in September 2009 (Pearl Jam's distribution deal for that album was an exclusive arrangement with Target, the band's first major-retailer-exclusive release). The song was therefore harder to find on conventional vinyl than other Backspacer material, which gave it an unusual collectible status among Pearl Jam fans for several years.

Live, 'Got Some' has been a setlist regular since 2009. The song works as a mid-set energy injection or as an early-show second-or-third position; it does not work as an opener or as a closer. In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Got Some' appeared at Morumbi on November 3 (sixth in the order), at Apoteose on November 6 (fourteenth), and at Curitiba on November 9 (sixteenth). The consistent appearances across three of the four nights, in three different positions, suggest the band was using the song as a flex point in setlist construction. The Brazilian audience response on the bootlegs is energetic but uneven; 'Got Some' was a more recent song than most of the Brazilian audience's strongest associations with the band, and the response varies by venue.
wma:
'W.M.A.' is the eighth track on Vs. (1993). The acronym in the title is the song's argument: White Male American. The music is credited to Jeff Ament and Dave Abbruzzese; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written in direct response to a real incident: Vedder and a Black friend were standing outside the Pearl Jam offices in Seattle when a police officer approached the two of them and singled out the friend for questioning while ignoring Vedder. The song is the thought experiment the moment generated. Vedder describes, in third-person address, a man who moves through the world without friction because of his racial demographic, and the song is the indictment of that frictionless movement.

The arrangement is the most rhythmically aggressive thing on Vs. Jeff Ament's bass line is the structural engine, and Dave Abbruzzese's drumming (this is one of two songs on Vs. where Abbruzzese receives co-writing credit, an unusual designation for a Pearl Jam record) builds a tribal-pulse texture that Vedder has compared, in interviews from the 1993 Vs. promotional cycle, to the rhythm vocabulary of Public Enemy's late-80s work. The song is therefore Pearl Jam's most explicit attempt to engage with hip-hop rhythmic priorities, and the result is unlike anything else in the band's catalog.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct political statements. The narrator names the demographic, names the privilege, and refuses to soften the indictment with personal mitigation. Vedder discussed the song's argument extensively during the Vitalogy tour of 1995 in stage introductions and in select interviews, framing the song as an attempt to make audible to white American audiences the racial weather they were inhabiting without noticing. The song does not offer redemption. It diagnoses.

Live, 'W.M.A.' has been a rare song. It appears in fewer than 200 shows in three decades of touring, partly because the rhythmic arrangement is difficult to land outside the studio environment and partly because the band has historically reserved the song for moments when its argument feels particularly necessary. The song is more often deployed as a tag during 'Daughter' than as a standalone performance, which lets the band fold the W.M.A. argument into the W.M.A.-adjacent argument of 'Daughter' (a song about another kind of demographic vulnerability).

In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'W.M.A.' appeared as the tag for 'Daughter' at Morumbi on November 3, the first SP show. The pairing is one of the most thoughtful sequencing choices on the South American Tour 2011 bootlegs. Brazilian audiences in 2011 had their own complicated relationship with the racial questions the song addresses (the Lula-era Brazil had passed Lei 12.288 in 2010, the Statute of Racial Equality, just a year before this show), and the band's decision to import a song this specific to American police violence into a Brazilian arena was a small act of trust in the audience's ability to translate the argument across hemispheres.
ole:
'Olé' is one of the few standalone single releases in the Pearl Jam catalog, distributed for free to members of the band's Ten Club fan organization in March 2011 ahead of the PJ20 Anniversary Tour. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was recorded in Henry Rollins's home studio in Los Angeles in early 2011 with the band on a quick session that did not produce a full album. 'Olé' was therefore a one-off release rather than a track from a larger record, which gives it a particular standing in the catalog.

The song's title and its central refrain reference the Spanish-language exclamation 'Olé,' which originated in flamenco performance traditions and which entered global stadium culture through bullfighting and football crowds. The song is, at the simplest level, a celebration song, written in 2011 when the band was preparing to celebrate its twentieth anniversary as a touring entity. The lyric is unusually optimistic for Vedder. The narrator is honoring a partner, honoring the persistence of a relationship across decades, honoring the kind of shared survival that becomes its own celebration.

The arrangement is one of the most pop-leaning things the band recorded in the 2010s. The chord progression is a clean four-bar pattern that does not deviate; the chorus opens into the wordless 'Olé' refrain that is designed to be carried by stadium audiences. Matt Cameron's drumming is a straight 4/4 with brushed accents. The song's accessibility is intentional. The band wanted a song that could function as a mid-show audience moment on the PJ20 tour, and 'Olé' was built for exactly that role.

Live, the song was a fixture of the 2011 PJ20 cycle and has appeared sporadically on subsequent tours. Its status as a free-download single rather than an album track gives it an unusual lifespan: it is well-known enough among fans that audiences sing the refrain, but is rarely heard on radio, and most casual Pearl Jam listeners have never heard it. This makes the song's live performance a kind of fan-club handshake: if you sing along, you announce yourself as a Ten Club member.

In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Olé' appeared in three of the four nights. At Morumbi on November 3 it was placed eleventh in the order. At Morumbi on November 4 it was placed twenty-second. At Curitiba on November 9 it was placed fourth. The varying positions suggest the band was experimenting with where the song landed best in a setlist, which is unusual for the PJ20 tour (most songs found a fixed slot). The Brazilian audience response was strongest at Curitiba, where the song's early placement gave the wordless refrain time to spread through the venue before the night's heavier material arrived. The bootleg recording from Vila Capanema captures one of the louder Olé refrains of the South American Tour 2011.
the fixer:
'The Fixer' is the third track on Backspacer (2009) and the album's lead single, released in August 2009 ahead of the September album release. The music is credited collectively to the band; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was the most commercially successful Pearl Jam single since 'Just Breathe' would land later in the same album cycle, and it reached number one on the Billboard Alternative Songs chart, the band's first chart-topper in that category since 'World Wide Suicide' in 2006.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most simple optimistic declarations. The narrator describes himself as someone who repairs what is broken, who restores what has been damaged, who restores what has gone missing. The song is, in deliberate contrast to almost every Pearl Jam track from the 2002 to 2006 period, a refusal of pessimism. Vedder discussed the song in a 2009 Rolling Stone interview around the Backspacer release as a song he had been wanting to write for years and had only been able to write after the Bush administration ended; the song's optimism is the optimism of someone who has been holding it back for half a decade.

The arrangement is the brightest thing on Backspacer. The verse is built on a major-key chord progression that climbs rather than descends; the chorus opens into a wider arrangement that includes glockenspiel and tambourine, instruments that almost never appear in the Pearl Jam catalog. The song is closer in spirit to The Who's 'Substitute' or to early 70s power-pop than to anything Pearl Jam had recorded before. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the song forward at a tempo that the band has only rarely sustained on a recording.

The song was produced by Brendan O'Brien, and his fingerprint is unusually visible on the recording. O'Brien has discussed in interviews from the 2009 Backspacer cycle that 'The Fixer' was the first song from the sessions to be finished, and that the band's enthusiasm for the recording set the tone for the rest of the album. The song therefore functions, structurally, as the album's emotional thesis: the entire Backspacer record is built around the optimistic posture that 'The Fixer' establishes.

Live, 'The Fixer' has been a setlist regular since 2009. The song works as an opener or as an early-set energy injection; it does not work as a closer. In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'The Fixer' appeared at Morumbi on November 3 (fourteenth in the order), at Apoteose on November 6 (twelfth), and at Curitiba on November 9 (tenth). The consistent placement in the early-middle of every show suggests the band had decided 'The Fixer' would mark the audience-warming-up moment in each Brazilian set. The Brazilian crowd's response is enthusiastic across all three bootlegs, which is consistent with the song's chart success in Brazil in 2009 (the song received heavy rotation on Brazilian alternative rock radio in the year of its release).
down:
'Down' is one of two songs (with 'Yellow Ledbetter' the other) released as B-sides during the Riot Act period that became, retroactively, more important to the band's catalog than most of the album they were supporting. The song was recorded during the Riot Act sessions in 2002 and was issued in November 2002 as the B-side to the 'I Am Mine' single. It was eventually collected on Lost Dogs (2003), the rarities compilation. The music is credited to Mike McCready; the lyric is Vedder's.

The lyric is one of the most direct political tracks Pearl Jam wrote during the Bush administration, and one of the most temporally specific. The song addresses someone (the second person 'you' is the political figure being indicted) who is dragging the country down, who is taking the worst available path, who is making the moment worse than it had to be. Vedder confirmed in a 2003 interview during the Riot Act tour that the song was about the Bush administration's response to 9/11 and the rush to war in Iraq. The song was written after the studio sessions for 'Bu$hleaguer' (also on Riot Act) and was not included on the album because the band felt the political content of Riot Act was already at saturation.

The arrangement is one of McCready's most economical pieces of writing. The verse is built on a tight, almost punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. The song is structured for velocity rather than for argument, and the lyric's anger is therefore delivered through the music's pace rather than through extended rhetorical development. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is among the most aggressive of the Riot Act sessions.

Live, 'Down' has been a regular but not heavy presence in setlists since 2003. The song's specific political target makes it most useful during American electoral cycles or during periods when the political climate the song was written about feels current again. The band has historically reserved 'Down' for shows where the lyric will resonate, which is unusual for a B-side that the band could have allowed to fade from the live catalog.

In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Down' appeared at Morumbi on November 3, twelfth in the running order, between 'Olé' and 'Save You.' The placement is one of the more thoughtful sequencing choices on the bootleg. Following 'Olé' (a celebration song) with 'Down' (a song of political indictment) and resolving into 'Save You' (a personal grief song) creates a three-song sequence that moves from communal joy to public anger to private mourning. The Brazilian audience response to 'Down' on the Morumbi recording is more measured than the response to the songs around it, which is consistent with how Brazilian audiences had received Riot Act material since the 2003 tour: the songs were respected rather than embraced.
severed hand:
'Severed Hand' is the fourth track on Pearl Jam (2006), the self-titled album often called Avocado for its cover image. The music is Mike McCready's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most stylistically unusual things on the album, a sustained psychedelic burst that draws openly from late-60s rock vocabulary (the Doors and the Jefferson Airplane are the two most-cited reference points) and applies that vocabulary to a lyric about a transformative drug experience. Pearl Jam had not previously recorded a song this explicitly about psychedelics, and they have not recorded one since.

The lyric describes a vision the narrator receives during an altered state. The vision is not described in detail; the song is more interested in the emotional aftermath than in the specifics of the experience. The narrator emerges from the vision changed, with a clarity about something that the song refuses to name. Vedder discussed the song in a 2006 Spin interview during the Avocado promotional cycle as 'a song about realizing something' but declined to specify what was realized. This refusal to specify is consistent with how psychedelic literature has historically described peak experiences: the experience cannot be communicated in the language available to non-experiencers, so the song chooses not to try.

The arrangement is one of McCready's most ambitious solo features. The intro is built on a wah-wah guitar figure that explicitly references Hendrix's 'Voodoo Chile (Slight Return),' and the closing solo extends McCready's Hendrix vocabulary into territory the band rarely allows him to explore in studio recordings. The song's psychedelic arrangement is therefore not just thematic decoration; it is the music doing the same work the lyric is doing, attempting to render in sound what the lyric refuses to render in language.

The song was produced by Adam Kasper rather than by Brendan O'Brien. Avocado is the only Pearl Jam album of the 2000s that O'Brien did not produce, and Kasper's production is audibly different: the recording is rawer, the rhythm section is more present, and McCready's guitar is mixed louder than O'Brien typically allows. 'Severed Hand' is the song where Kasper's production approach is most visible, and the result is one of the most distinctive-sounding tracks in the post-2000 Pearl Jam catalog.

Live, 'Severed Hand' has been a regular but not heavy presence since 2006. The song works best in the first half of a set, where its velocity and McCready feature can establish the show's energy. In the 2011 Brazilian shows, 'Severed Hand' appeared at Morumbi on November 4 (third in the order) and at Curitiba on November 9 (third again). The consistent third-position placement across both nights suggests the band had decided 'Severed Hand' would mark the show's first guitar-feature moment, and the bootleg recordings confirm that McCready's solo at this position landed each night with the kind of intensity that is harder to sustain in mid-set or encore positions.
